title: Demand
objective: After this level you can explain why buyers want less of something when its price rises.
summary: The law of demand: a higher price almost always cuts the quantity demanded, through the substitution and income effects. Income, tastes and related prices shift the whole demand curve.

cards.headline: When gas prices jump, people start carpooling.
cards.body: Nobody orders them to. They combine errands, take the bus and plan trips closer to home. Each person quietly buys a bit less. Add them all up and you get a law of economics.

cards.headline: The law of demand
cards.body: A rise in price almost always cuts the quantity demanded, the amount buyers want at that price. A fall in price raises it. It's Level 42's law in the mirror: when prices climb, sellers want to sell more and buyers want to buy less. Draw it and the demand curve slopes downward, because people buy more when things are cheaper.

cards.headline: Two reasons you buy less
cards.body: First, the substitution effect: when one thing gets pricier, you switch toward things that are now relatively cheaper, like the bus instead of the car. Second, the income effect: a higher price shrinks what your money can buy, even though your pay hasn't changed, so you buy less of most goods. Two effects, one direction.

mascot.line: Same paycheck, pricier gas. Your wallet just shrank without losing a cent.

cards.fact: Demand can change even when the price stands still.
cards.context: Like supply, the demand curve holds other things equal. Change them and the whole curve shifts: income, tastes, the prices of related goods, population, even expectations about the future. A change in the good's own price just slides buyers along the curve, exactly as Level 42's sellers slide along theirs.

cards.headline: Demand: understood
learned: Higher price, less wanted: the law of demand
Substitution and income effects explain it
Income and tastes shift the whole curve

questions.prompt: What does the law of demand say?

options.label: When a price rises, sellers offer more
When a price rises, buyers want less of it
Buyers always want the same amount
options.rationale: The amount buyers want changes with the price.

options.label: Higher prices make people want more
options.rationale: It works the other way for almost all goods.

questions.explanation: A rise in price almost always decreases the quantity demanded; a fall increases it.

questions.prompt: Gas prices jump but bus fares stay put, so you ride the bus more. What is this called?

options.label: The income effect
options.rationale: That one is about your money buying less overall.

options.label: The law of supply
options.rationale: That's about sellers, not your choice of transport.

options.label: A price floor
options.rationale: No legal minimum price is involved here.

questions.explanation: Switching toward a good that is now relatively cheaper is the substitution effect.

questions.prompt: Your income rises and you buy more concert tickets, though ticket prices haven't changed. In Level 42's terms, what happened?

options.label: You moved along the demand curve
options.rationale: Moving along needs a change in the price itself.

options.label: The supply curve shifted
options.rationale: Nothing changed for sellers; it's your demand.

options.label: The law of demand stopped working
options.rationale: The law still holds; the whole curve moved.

questions.explanation: A change in income is one of the other things held equal. When it changes, the whole demand curve shifts.
